item.title: Microsoft struggles to get M365 services back online after widespread outage
item.description:
If you’re struggling to send or receive emails, you’re not alone. Microsoft has been unable to fully restore Microsoft 365 more than 13 hours after an Exchange Online failure took down Outlook and spread to Teams, SharePoint, Copilot and parts of the company’s security tooling, and it said overnight that its latest fixes were “not taking as expected.”

The outage began at 16:17 UTC on Nov. 12, according to Microsoft’s service health dashboard.

“Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed,” Microsoft wrote in the dashboard.

Users in the Americas could not reach their mailboxes through Outlook on the web, desktop Outlook, mobile clients, or the REST API. Within two hours, Microsoft said users in any region could be affected. It opened a wider incident covering Teams, SharePoint Online, Copilot, Defender XDR, Intune, Power BI, and several Purview services.

Downdetector logged more than 130,000 Outlook problem reports at the peak.

In its latest service-health updates for incident MO1550821, Microsoft said it had observed a surge in calls from routing services to backend servers as it applied mitigation measures. The company said traffic rebalancing had contributed to the increased volume and that it was scaling virtual machines to add capacity and reduce the load.

“As we’ve applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers,” Microsoft said in the update. It added: “We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event.”

Server failures behind the disruption

Microsoft initially investigated elevated infrastructure load and the possibility that a recent change had contributed to the incident. It later said the problem was not being driven by an overall increase in traffic.

“We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure,” the company said in its Exchange Online incident update.

In a subsequent update, Microsoft identified a process responsible for establishing secure connections as a source of the problem.

“Our investigation has found that a process on the affected servers responsible for establishing secure connections becomes overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop processing requests,” the company said.

Microsoft said it was preparing a configuration change to address the behaviour and testing it on a subset of servers before wider deployment. It was also reverting a recent network configuration change that correlated with the start of the disruption, while restarting affected infrastructure and monitoring server stability.

The recovery process has involved restricting some traffic and gradually reintroducing connections as Microsoft checks whether servers can remain stable under load. The company also reported that some servers became unresponsive again after traffic was restored, requiring further analysis and mitigation.

Impact extends beyond email

Microsoft’s incident notification said the impact varied by service and feature, depending in part on whether they relied on Exchange Online.

The company said users might be unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes through Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop, Exchange ActiveSync, or REST-based connections, and that email delivery might be delayed. It said Teams’ core messaging and online meetings remained largely functional, but Exchange-dependent features such as calendar access and meeting scheduling could fail.

Microsoft also said that direct access to files stored in SharePoint Online remained functional, while features dependent on Exchange Online could be affected. For Microsoft 365 Copilot, users might be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses, and Copilot experiences might be unable to access work data such as email, calendars, and files.

The notification also identified potential impacts to Defender for Office 365 Safe Links, which might be unable to verify URLs clicked in Outlook and Teams, and to some Defender XDR portal pages. Other reported impacts included selected Intune device enrolment and compliance scenarios and Purview functions such as data loss prevention, automatic labelling and communication compliance.

Enterprise concentration risk

The incident has renewed attention on the operational dependencies created when organisations consolidate email, collaboration and security functions within a single cloud ecosystem.

“Enterprises have priced Microsoft 365 as a licence and never as a single point of failure,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research.

Gogia said that when mail, meetings and security functions such as Safe Links depend on the same service estate, an infrastructure disruption can affect several business functions at once.

“The answer is not a second suite. It is a rehearsed fallback for the few things that cannot stop: an out-of-band channel for incident command, mail continuity for critical roles, and a written decision on whether each security control fails open or closed,” he said.

For security teams, the distinction between a service being unavailable and a dependent security function being impaired is important. Microsoft’s notification about Safe Links, for example, points to a specific URL-verification impact rather than the loss of all Defender for Office 365 capabilities.

Gogia also said enterprise customers would want a detailed account of the incident, including a timeline showing when Microsoft identified the different causes and how it validated the recovery measures. Microsoft has continued to publish updates through its Microsoft 365 service status portal. The company has not yet published a final post-incident root-cause report.

item.title: United Airlines becomes the latest enterprise to shut its door to customer bots
item.description:
United Airlines on Wednesday became the latest enterprise to block customer bots, following similar moves from Walmart, Target and Amazon. 

The $59 billion airline, the second largest in the world, said the move was prompted by fears of data leakage, unintended purchases, and the risk of violating federal airline rules. 

But industry observers say that the more concerning business risks are the lack of industry standardization around AI coupled with an ever-increasing number of bots from major AI vendors and AI startups. The fear is that supporting the multiple bots that customers use could become an almost infinite drain on IT resources. However, they said, strictly enforced industry standards might persuade some enterprises to rethink their bot resistance. 

United’s statement said, “United is taking steps to restrict access – directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators – to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants. This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.”

It pointed out that corporate leaders in the banking and retail industries have taken similar actions regarding AI agents, and said, “we encourage others to consider measures that preserve the data and security of their customers and strengthen safety.”

The airline listed a variety of problems with bots that it is trying to avoid, including the risks associated with customers sharing account credentials “with personal, third-party, AI assistants [that] can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.”

It also spoke of regulatory challenges: “These automated AI actions have the potential to violate FAA [United States Federal Aviation Administration] and DOT [US Department of Transportation] regulations,” such as those stating that flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.

However, the airline sent a clear signal to the industry that it was willing to reconsider the ban if there are sufficient changes. “As personal AI assistants evolve, United will continue to evaluate how these tools interact with our services, with a focus on protecting our customers,” the statement said.

Separating the humans from the bots

One of the bigger enterprise concerns about agents is that, because they are using the customer’s credentials, the bot activity is typically indistinguishable from the human customer’s activity. Analysts say that the cleanest way to address that is to simply assign bots their own credentials.

Last month, Walmart got close to that goal, putting in place a program, scheduled to start this month, to try to differentiate bot and human actions.

“Today, when a customer uses an AI agent, it signs in using a customer’s account. This means that all purchases – whether made by the customer or the agent – appear together, without any differentiation,” its announcement said. “Agent Profiles, launching in the next month, will offer a new level of transparency for customers. Customers will be able to authorize each AI agent with a dedicated profile within the customer’s account, so the customers will be able to see the agent’s purchases separately from the rest of their purchases.”

Target, on the other hand, blocked all but a handful of approved agents in recent changes to its terms and conditions, granting access only to Target’s AI Shopping Assistant, OAI, Google and Microsoft, although it said it may ”add, remove, or otherwise modify the list of Approved Agents at any time and in its sole discretion.”

Any other agentic commerce tools, it said, “are unauthorized, expressly prohibited, and may not be used to access, log into, scrape, query, or otherwise interact with or gather data from the Site under any circumstances, whether directly or through API call(s), automated use of user credentials, or other means” and approved agents may not be used in combination with unauthorized ones unless explicitly approved by Target, in writing.

Reducing risk

Although analysts and consultants agreed that they expect many more enterprises to block external bot access, their opinions were mixed on whether these blocks would meaningfully dilute the value of autonomous agents, especially those making purchases, ordering plane tickets or performing related concierge functions.

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, said, “blocking does not destroy the value of agents. It moves it. Every wall eventually gets a gate. The gate charges admission.”

He pointed out that United’s own wording points there: it prohibits unauthorized agents, which leaves room for authorized ones. “Expect agent access to come back through channels the enterprise controls, on the enterprise’s terms,” he said. “Whoever owns the agent owns the customer relationship. Airlines have spent years pulling customers back from third-party travel sites. They are not going to hand that relationship to someone else’s chatbot.”

He added that enterprises are just trying to reduce risk.

“Enterprises do not fear bots. They fear liability that nobody has assigned,” Dickson said. “Once a rule says which steps a human must perform, which steps an agent may perform, and how each is recorded, a general counsel can sign off on the deployment. Ambiguity is what keeps bots stuck in pilot.”

He noted that the complexity of having an unlimited number of different agents visiting is too risky. 

“A sea of agents is a sea of requests. Somebody pays for every one,” he said. “Every new agent arrives with its own way of logging in, its own idea of what the customer approved, and its own record of what it did, if it keeps one at all. An airline cannot build a separate door for each of them. Nobody should expect it to. Saying no until the market settles down is a reasonable risk decision. Bots that check prices over and over do not buy more seats.”

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, added that there’s no downside to United’s ban. 

“United is in a position where there is substantial risk, an uncertain commercial upside, and almost no competitive pressure to accept either,” he said. “In that type of position, they are able to take the approach of waiting for the legal consequences of bot behavior to become more predictable before they allow it.”

Limits needed

Kenney said one of his biggest concerns is the lack of effective limits on what a bot can do.

“One of the biggest mistakes I see in enterprise AI deployments is giving agents access to far more information and systems than their responsibilities actually require,” Kenney said. “There is a fundamental difference between an agent that is instructed to access only one system and an agent that is technically incapable of accessing anything else. We shouldn’t be giving agents broad capabilities and hoping they exercise restraint.”

Because of this, Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, said he expects more companies to impose restrictions on bots while they establish controls on their use, noting, “widespread blocking would reduce agents’ value by preventing them from completing tasks across services.”

He added that customer training in bot realities could also be quite helpful.

“People need to understand that actions they authorize through an agent can still create obligations for them, even when they never personally click ‘buy,’ ‘send’ or ‘confirm,’” Greis said. “I expect a substantial cultural shift here: just as people may say things online they would never say face to face, agents could create a similar distance between someone’s choices and their sense of responsibility.”

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.

item.title: The midterms are over. The business fallout is just beginning
item.description:
Within six days of the November 3 midterm election, investors had repriced healthcare companies, banks were preparing for a different oversight environment and analysts had lowered the odds of a major energy-permitting bill. No new Congress had convened. No sweeping banking law had been rewritten. No healthcare funding compromise had been enacted.

A change in law is not required for the economics of a business decision to change. Investors, counterparties and management teams revise expectations as the probability of different outcomes shifts. Those expectations influence choices being made now.

Across manufacturing, financial services and enterprise technology, I have seen decisions that made sense within one function create expensive problems for another. That risk grows when capital and specialist capacity are already committed. Following this election, the CEO needs to understand strategic exposure, the CFO needs to test the financial implications and the COO needs to determine what can actually be delivered. Those assessments belong in the same conversation, while there is still room to change course.

The vote is complete. The effects on enterprise plans are still taking shape.

6 days that changed the planning assumptions

The Associated Press confirmed Democratic control of both chambers, with the new majorities due to take office in January 2027. The immediate market response illustrated how quickly expectations can change before policy does.

On November 4, shares of Medicaid- and Affordable Care Act-exposed insurers rallied on hopes that the incoming Congress might slow planned Medicaid reductions or revive enhanced coverage subsidies. Centene closed up 12.6% and Molina Healthcare gained 8.9%, according to Becker’s post-election market review. These were changes in investor expectations, not evidence that future reimbursements had already increased.

The same week, banks began identifying which activities could attract congressional attention. Reuters reported on November 5 that financial institutions were examining exposure to investigations involving consumer fees, lending, fraud and regulatory relief. There had been no sudden reversal of existing capital rules; the anticipated change was in oversight, political leverage and the cost of being unprepared.

On November 9, an energy permitting proposal became an early test of the new political environment. Reuters reported that TD Cowen had cut its estimated chance of passage from 40% before the election to 25% afterward. The bill’s fate remained undecided, but the revised probability mattered to electricity infrastructure and data-center investment plans.

The clocks move at different speeds. Investors can revise valuations within hours, while policy changes and operational responses unfold over months. Continuing to use the old assumptions until new rules are final is itself a decision. In capital-intensive businesses, that decision can become costly.

Four sectors, four channels of exposure

  • Banking: oversight before legislation. A bank’s near-term exposure is not limited to whether Congress passes new rules. Committee investigations, potential hearings, consumer-fee scrutiny and renewed debate over digital assets can redirect legal, compliance and management capacity before a statute changes. A CFO might need to revisit the economics of consumer products or a pending acquisition; a COO may need to reserve the same risk, technology and operations teams already committed to modernization. The long-term scenarios include changes to consumer protection, bank mergers and regulatory priorities, but the immediate response is an assessment of vulnerability, not a prediction of enacted rules.
  • Insurance: coverage economics and affordability. Health insurers must plan for divergent enrollment, subsidy and Medicaid pathways while updating provider contracts, network capacity and service systems. Meanwhile, property and casualty carriers face political attention to premium affordability, disaster resilience and federal flood programs. Insurance industry representatives interviewed after the election emphasized bipartisan priorities, underscoring that risk exposure does not follow a simple partisan forecast. Repricing, reinsurance, claims capacity and regulatory engagement operate on different timelines.
  • Healthcare: the cash-flow consequences of coverage uncertainty. Hospitals and health systems are especially exposed to reimbursement, payer mix and uncompensated care. A funding decision in Washington can eventually alter the economics of staffing, rural service lines, digital access or capital expansion. But the underlying pressures predate this election. KFF’s November 6 analysis found that finalized benchmark marketplace premiums for 2027 were up an average of 13%, while prior subsidy expirations and coverage rules were already affecting the enrollment outlook. The executive task is to distinguish conditions already embedded in the forecast from policy alternatives that could change it.
  • Pharmaceuticals: pricing, access and capital allocation. Drug manufacturers face possible congressional scrutiny of pricing agreements, pharmacy benefit managers and government relationships, while tariff policy, FDA decisions and manufacturing-location choices remain active through executive agencies. PwC’s post-election industry assessment identifies drug-pricing pressure, trade policy, development modernization and supply-chain exposure as interacting forces. A favorable legislative outcome in one area would not eliminate risks in another. The decisions concern portfolio economics, investment timing, contracting and supply-chain resilience—not simply compliance with the next announcement.

The common thread across these sectors is how quickly a policy expectation can become an operating constraint. A hospital anticipating lower reimbursement may defer capital spending. That can delay a technology investment or alter staffing plans. Each decision may be defensible on its own while the combined result weakens the organization’s position. Executives need to understand the net effect.

The next shock is likely to arrive before the last one is resolved

Divided government does not mean the policy environment stands still. The White House retains executive and rulemaking authority; Congress can use appropriations, confirmation powers, investigations and oversight. State governments and regulators can move on separate tracks. Some measures may be blocked, others negotiated and still others implemented administratively.

PwC’s November 4 assessment cautions that political control does not remove uncertainty for business. For executives, the practical implication is to plan across time horizons: immediate market and reputational exposure; next-quarter decisions on staffing, pricing and capital; and longer-horizon changes to regulation, investment economics and customer demand.

The election also sits within a broader pattern of overlapping geopolitical, technology and economic disruptions. In McKinsey’s 2026 survey of 202 executives and other senior respondents, 53% said strategic foresight approaches would materially strengthen geopolitical resilience, yet fewer than 30% reported using them to guide decisions. Just 5% said their organizations had conducted simulations of geopolitical exposure and response.

The survey cannot tell us how often the next disruption will come. It does suggest that relatively few organizations have made the testing of response options a routine management practice. That is a significant weakness when one event can change the assumptions supporting several major investments at once.

The management advantage is shorter, more accurate decision cycles

Speed is valuable only if it improves the decision. A quick response built on incomplete assumptions can be as damaging as one delivered too late. The aim is to reduce the time between a material event and a decision that has been tested against credible alternatives, resource limits and financial consequences.

In executive planning discussions, I rarely find much disagreement that a new priority matters. The difficult question is what gives way. A regulatory deadline may be nonnegotiable, but the architects, compliance specialists and operations teams needed to meet it are already supporting other commitments. Until that displacement is understood, approval of the new priority is only part of the decision.

Three changes in management practice follow from this.

  1. Define triggers rather than wait for certainty. Management should identify the policy, pricing, funding or market developments that would materially change a decision. A proposed Medicaid revision, a supervisory hearing, a drug-pricing rule or an infrastructure-permitting delay should activate a predetermined review—not an improvised search for who owns the issue.
  2. Model enterprise effects, not isolated exposures. The CFO needs changes in cash flow, capital requirements and expected return; the COO needs effects on service continuity, supply chains, shared capacity and sequencing; the CEO needs to know which commitments should be protected, revised or abandoned. Options need to be compared using common assumptions, with uncertainty visible rather than buried in a single forecast.
  3. Establish decision rights and preserve the audit trail. Scenario analysis should show what was known, what was assumed, which alternatives were considered and why leadership acted. This improves the next decision as well as accountability for the last one.

Technology can compress the time needed to gather evidence and test alternatives, but it cannot substitute for judgment. In an October 2026 McKinsey analysis of the strategic judgment bottleneck, the authors warn that faster AI analysis does not automatically produce faster, better decisions. Trust in assumptions, the ability to challenge outputs and the willingness to reallocate people and capital remain decisive.

The economic case for continuous scenario planning follows from that discipline. Leadership needs a current view of how its choices interact with resources, obligations and expected financial outcomes. I think of it as an enterprise net-change calculation: what a decision makes possible, what it consumes and what it displaces. Used consistently, it can flag cash-flow exposure earlier, reduce avoidable conflicts over scarce capacity and help executives compare investments without repeatedly reconstructing the entire plan.

Making resilience an operating capability

The first six days after November 3 did not determine the final direction of U.S. policy. They showed how quickly market expectations and business assumptions can move before the legislative process has meaningfully begun.

The next phase will unfold on several tracks at once: funding negotiations, congressional oversight, agency action and state-level initiatives. Some forecasts will be wrong. Other developments will affect multiple industries in combinations that today’s estimates do not fully capture.

The executive challenge is to bring three legitimate perspectives to the same decision. The CEO considers strategic exposure. The CFO tests the economics and opportunity cost. The COO asks whether the operating model can absorb the change. I have seen teams reach agreement on direction while still holding different assumptions about what execution would require. Making those assumptions explicit is often the point at which a decision becomes workable.

An executive team cannot know exactly which disruption will come next. It can establish how quickly to assess the implications, which assumptions to test and who has authority to act. When those practices are part of ordinary management, the organization does not have to rebuild its decision process with every new shock. That is a practical definition of resilience.

item.title: Inside X-VPN’s 200%+ Speed Upgrade: 25 Gbps Servers, AI Routing and Talaria Protocol
item.description:
Internal 10 Gbps tests showed over 200% aggregate improvement in download and upload speeds with Talaria.

X-VPN has rolled out a speed upgrade spanning its network and new in-house Talaria protocol. In the company’s internal 10 Gbps tests, Talaria delivered over 200% aggregate improvement in download and upload speeds compared with X-VPN’s previous best-performing protocols.

Alongside higher-bandwidth server infrastructure, X-VPN has improved route selection and how devices and servers process traffic. The changes are designed to make connections more efficient, from initial setup to sustained data transfer.

Expanding Server Capacity to 25 Gbps

X-VPN has introduced servers with 25 Gbps port capacity in the United States and Canada, alongside 10 Gbps infrastructure in Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, the UK, Italy, and Singapore. More than 90% of X-VPN’s VPN traffic in the US and Europe can now be served by 10 Gbps or 25 Gbps infrastructure.

Beyond bandwidth, X-VPN has also upgraded its computing hardware. Its new bare-metal server configurations feature 64 CPU cores and 128–256 GB of memory, providing greater processing capacity to handle simultaneous connections and large volumes of network traffic.

The additional bandwidth and computing resources give X-VPN more headroom to handle demanding traffic loads and support high-throughput connections.

X-VPN’s Speed Tests Show

X-VPN conducted internal speed tests across Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS, with connections originating in Singapore and reaching VPN servers in Singapore, the UK, and the US.

Across the 10 Gbps test configurations, Talaria achieved over 200% aggregate improvement in download and upload speeds compared with X-VPN’s previous best-performing protocols.

For example, in 10 Gbps Windows tests connecting to a Singapore VPN server, median download speed increased from 1,536 Mbps with the previous protocol to 5,706 Mbps with Talaria.

In separate 1 Gbps tests measuring speed loss against connections without a VPN, Talaria kept download speed loss below 2% on both Windows and macOS across the tested locations in Singapore, the UK, and the US.

These results reflect X-VPN’s internal testing under defined configurations. Actual performance may vary depending on the device, network environment, and VPN server.

Improving Data Transfers Across Devices

X-VPN has also streamlined its client and server data paths to reduce unnecessary data copying, repeated processing, and resource contention.

On Windows, an upgraded kernel data driver helps improve processing efficiency. On macOS, more balanced multicore scheduling keeps CPU cores productive while reducing competition for shared resources. Android and iOS use larger data batches on supported paths, allowing more information to be processed in each cycle with fewer repeated operations.

On the server side, X-VPN has introduced prefetching, batched writes, and more efficient forwarding for eligible traffic. These techniques reduce repeated processing and data handoffs, helping the system make better use of its computing resources during sustained transfers.

How AI Routing Reduces Unnecessary Connection Attempts

X-VPN’s SmartEntry Adaptive Mesh evaluates available high-capacity entry nodes and network conditions to help select a suitable connection path.

Its AI Routing technology, PrivacyRoute Fabric, prioritizes promising connection candidates in time-limited batches rather than attempting every available server. Once a candidate successfully authenticates, the remaining attempts stop.

This approach reduces unnecessary connection attempts and is designed to help users establish suitable VPN connections with less waiting.

Talaria’s Multi-Channel and Parallel Processing Design

Talaria, X-VPN’s new in-house protocol, is designed to make more efficient use of available bandwidth by reducing repeated work during data transmission.

Instead of placing concurrent application connections into a single shared processing path, Talaria gives each connection its own transport channel. Multiple streams can then be processed independently across CPU cores, reducing competition for processing resources when several applications are active.

Talaria also handles data packets in batches, processing multiple packets in a single operation rather than repeating the same steps for each one. Its processing pipeline separates receiving, decryption, and writing data back into stages that can operate independently.

On supported paths, flow-level forwarding further reduces packet-by-packet processing by reconstructing connection flows and forwarding their data more directly.

“Improving VPN speed involves more than adding bandwidth to servers,” said Julian Kwek, Cybersecurity Engineer at X-VPN. “We also looked at how data moves through the connection, from the device to the server and through the transport protocol. By reducing repeated processing at each stage, we can make better use of the bandwidth already available.”

Beyond Speed: Talaria’s Security Audit and Open-Source Release

Talaria incorporates security mechanisms including TLS 1.3, hybrid post-quantum key exchange, authenticated encryption, and replay protection.

The protocol underwent an independent security assessment by Singapore-based Vantage Point Security, including a white-box source code review and protocol-level penetration test. The assessment identified no security vulnerabilities. Four observations were addressed, with their resolution independently verified by Vantage Point Security. Within the scope and limitations of the assessment, the reviewed design and use of cryptography were also found to align with security best practices.

X-VPN has also open-sourced Talaria under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL v3). Its codebase is publicly available on GitHub for developers, security researchers, and the wider community to review.

Availability

The speed upgrade covers X-VPN’s Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS applications. Talaria is available to both free and premium users, with supported optimizations and performance varying by platform and network conditions.

About X-VPN

X-VPN is a VPN service focused on providing private internet connections across desktop and mobile platforms. Its ongoing development includes network infrastructure improvements, in-house protocol engineering, and independent security assessments.

item.title: CEOs have had enough of incremental AI
item.description:
Four years into the new AI era, and few business leaders appear happy with the results.

At issue is growing impatience with IT leaders who have not moved their organizations beyond using AI for small tweaks to current business process.

Seventy-seven percent of business decision-makers, including C-suite leaders, directors, and managers, believe their organizations are dedicating too much of their AI investments to incremental improvements, according to a survey commissioned by Microsoft-focused IT advisory services provider Avanade.

Only 11% of decision-makers expect AI to fundamentally change how their organizations operate, create value, or compete in the next year. Nearly two-thirds say AI has not yet delivered returns that justify their investment and effort, and three-quarters believe their organizations have overstated their AI maturity.

The survey shows that many organizations — and their CIOs — aren’t yet embracing the potential of AI, even though they see the possibilities, says Ben Beath, Avanade’s chief AI officer.

“Confidence is high, but confidence isn’t the same as change,” he adds. “Having Copilot licenses and a few dozen use cases can feel to a leader like maturity, but it probably isn’t if it hasn’t changed the way the work is actually getting done.”

When business leaders don’t see major returns from their AI investments, it suggests their organizations still haven’t reached AI maturity, he says, likely due to a misguided AI strategy and approach.

“That’s the product of bolting AI onto either broken or legacy processes,” he adds. “You just get a faster legacy process.”

Is your AI strategy transformational enough?

Instead of looking at ways to reinvent their businesses through AI, many IT leaders are chasing tools that summarize email messages or generate basic reports, Beath suggests. The basic uses of AI can significantly improve employee productivity, but they won’t transform the organization, he adds.

“Leaders aren’t confused about this,” he says. “They can see they’re stuck in efficiency and productivity mode when it comes to AI. The issue isn’t awareness; it’s that incremental projects are easier to approve, they’re easier to measure, and they’re a lot less risky for whoever sponsors them.”

But to be truly transformational, AI needs fully integrated into the business instead of bolted on to existing processes, he adds. And leading CIOs are doing just that, reimagining their organizations’ business processes to reap AI’s true benefits.

“The clients that are building AI into their business aren’t thinking about how they can add AI incrementally on top of an existing workflow,” he explains. “They’re saying, ‘What would this process in our business look like if it was reimagined with AI?’ and AI is embedded in every step of the way.”

Leadership gap

As Beath sees it, the majority of organizations are suffering from a leadership crisis, leaving CIOs to pursue AI projects without a broader leadership coalition getting involved.

“This is a leadership conversation and it’s not just an IT one,” he adds. “If AI strategy sits only with the CIO, there’s more of a focus on efficiency. If it sits with the CEO or the CFO and business leaders working in partnership with the CIO, you get AI transformation.”

CIOs, working with other business leaders, shouldn’t ask where they can use AI, but what business they would build today if they started from scratch with AI, Beath advises.

Not all CIOs spearheading AI strategies are focused solely on incremental gains. According to CIO.com’s State of the CIO survey, 59% of IT leaders report that some or most of their AI initiatives have met or exceeded ROI goals, with some even bringing AI transformation home to IT workflows.

But if more IT leaders focus on these more transformational uses of AI, rather than siloed efficiencies, they can turn the tide at their own organizations, bringing greater AI maturity and better business results, Beath adds.

“It’s not because the models are bad or because the pilots are poorly selected; it’s because the hard parts of AI are where data meets the app, or where technology meets the process, or where it meets the business,” he says. “AI transformation needs someone thinking across all of those, not just focused on the tech piece.”

Not an either-or proposition

CIOs may miss out on AI’s potential if they focus on incremental initiatives instead of transformational projects, but they don’t have to choose one or the other. In fact, many IT leaders, such as Ed Keisling, chief AI officer at Progress Software, believe the key to advancing the organization is using AI for both.

“I believe they go hand in hand,” he says. “The incremental improvements allow organizations to begin to explore the art of the possible with AI, and in some instances, can compound across an entire workflow to bring transformational results.”

The company is using AI agents, for example, to synthesize updates from its workplace collaboration, project management, and knowledge management systems to generate updates for leadership. Its sales organization also uses agents to synthesize data from the company’s CRM, data platforms, and customer systems to generate quotes more quickly and accurately, he says.

Progress Software is also deploying AI for more transformational purposes, including how the company handles requests for information and requests for proposals.

“These are extremely time-consuming processes that used to take days and now can be completed in minutes,” Keisling says. “It allows us to be more responsive to opportunities.”

Still, scaling AI tools across the organization can be tricky, he adds. In addition, several issues, including data sovereignty, security, and cost, hold organizations back from more transformational AI use cases, he says.

“Theres still a big challenge in scaling AI tooling from the individual to a team, and then to a team of teams or an organization,” Keisling says. “A lot of this has to do with how organizations want to manage the risk — which could be the risk of inaction as much as the risk of action — against the opportunities and threats that they perceive in the market.”

Meanwhile, the continuing elusiveness of AI ROI means IT leaders must be hyper focused on budgets and results, he adds. However, ROI doesn’t come only from transformational projects.

“If AI takes meaningful time out of a high-volume workflow, increases throughput, improves quality, or frees capacity, that can create significant economic value without being labeled ‘transformational,’” Keisling says.

Start small and build

Digital adoption software provider WalkMe has also found both incremental and transformational uses for AI, says Tal Carmi, the CIO there. The company started with incremental uses but is evolving as it goes, he adds.

“Incremental improvements are the steppingstones to transformation,” he says. “We have some areas where we started with AI-based solutions such as Copilot and after seeing the success rate, they evolved into auto pilot, transforming how work is done.”

Still, WalkMe has more work to do before most of its AI uses are transformational, Carmi says.

“In some areas, we’re already there and in others, we are not there yet,” he adds. “What’s holding us back is a combination of systems limitations, processes involving face to face interactions, risk ownership, and employee enablement.”

Many organizations appear to be held back by issues that plagued them before they had AI, he suggests.

“AI only magnifies your knowledge and data problems,” Carmi says. “Telling your LLM to extract data and build a dashboard is easy, making sure it extracts the right data and processes it the right way is a different story.”

Legacy systems also create roadblocks, he adds. “Many of the systems people most want to automate don’t have an API and are unlikely to get one anytime soon,” he says. “So people improvise, and that’s how shadow IT gets in.”

item.title: Top 10 IT certifications in demand today
item.description:
What are IT certifications?

IT certifications are professional designations offered by organizations and companies to help you demonstrate to employers your qualifications in specific skills, tools, and IT areas. To gain certifications, you’ll need to pass an exam, along with any other requirements set by the accrediting body. Gaining the right IT certifications for your role and industry can help you advance your career.

Certifications give you the opportunity to earn a credential in skills you already have or to grow your competencies by developing new skills you’d like to use in your career. Whatever your reason for getting certified, certifications are a great way to strengthen your resume, set yourself apart from other candidates in a job search, and boost your salary.

The significance of IT certifications

IT certifications not only help solidify the skills on your resume, but they can also offer education and hands-on experience. Many certifications require completing a course or training program, allowing you to learn new skills and hone existing ones. This can be a great opportunity for entry-level workers who need to bulk up their resumes or for more seasoned IT pros to set themselves apart from other candidates by validating their expertise and skills.

While some certifications consist of only an exam, many teach you new concepts, ideas, and expand your knowledge prior to certifying your skills and abilities. This can give you the opportunity to not only obtain an industry-recognized designation but also help you gain new skills and expertise for your resume.

IT certifications can boost salary in 2027

Overall, 72% of technology leaders say they’re planning to make more competitive offers for IT professionals in the new year, with 65% willing to offer salaries higher than the planned range to “secure candidates with specialized skills.” In 2027, 92% of IT leaders plan to offer higher salaries for relevant AI skills, and 60% plan to offer “more for AI-related expertise than any other tech skill,” according to the 2027 Salary Guide from Robert Half.

One of the easiest ways to demonstrate that you have specialized or specific skill sets that businesses are looking for is by earning an IT certification.

10 in-demand certifications for 2027

According to Robert Half’s 2027 Salary Guide, the following certifications are among the most valuable credentials IT professionals can hold today. Whether you’re just starting out and building your resume or you’ve been in the industry for 20 years, there’s a certification that can help boost your salary and your career:

  • AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner
  • Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP)
  • Certified Data Professional (CDP)
  • Certified Information Systems Auditor (CISA)
  • CompTIA A+
  • CompTIA Cloud+
  • CompTIA Security
  • IBM AI Engineering Professional Certificate
  • Microsoft Certified Azure Solutions Architect
  • Project Management Professional (PMP)

AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner

The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner certification covers the basics of AWS cloud, including its global infrastructure and architectural principles. You’ll be asked to define and describe the AWS cloud value proposition, key services on the AWS platform and their common use cases, as well as basic security and compliance aspects of the AWS platform and shared security model. It’s recommended that you have a basic understanding of IT services and how they work with AWS. You’ll also need at least six months of experience with AWS in any role, whether technical, managerial, sales, purchasing, or financial.

The average salary for IT professionals with an AWS Cloud Practitioner certification is $85,866 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $100

Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP)

The Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certification is offered through the International Information System Security Certification Consortium (ISC2) and demonstrates your knowledge and abilities when designing, managing, and securing data, applications, and infrastructure in the cloud. It’s designed for those working with cloud technology, including enterprise architects, security administrators, systems engineers, security architects, systems architects, consultants, engineers, or managers. The certification exam covers cloud concepts, architecture, design, security, and risk and compliance. While not required, the ISC2 recommends at least five years of experience in IT, with at least three years in information security and one year in one or more of the six domains found in the CCSP CBOK. For more, see “CCSP certification: Exam, cost, requirements, training, salary.”

The average salary for IT professionals with a CCSP certification is $122,000 per year, according to data from Payscale.

Exam fee: $599

Certified Data Professional (CDP)

Available from the Institute for Certification of Computing Professionals (ICCP), the Certified Data Professional (CDP) certification offers several learning paths. CDP candidates can choose from a range of domains, including business analytics, data analytics and design, data governance, data integration and interoperability, data management, data warehousing, enterprise data architecture, information systems or IT management, and more. The CDP is offered at various levels starting with Foundation and moving on to Associate, Mastery, Principal, and ending at the final level of Executive Management.

The average salary for IT professionals with a CDP certification is $118,445 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $1,050 for the basic professional exam package

Certified Information Systems Auditor (CISA)

Offered through ISACA, the Certified Information Systems Auditor (CISA) certification is a globally recognized certification for IS audit control. It was established in 1978 and certifies your ability to report on compliance procedures, how well you can assess vulnerabilities, and your knowledge of every stage in the auditing process. To qualify, you need at least five years of experience in IS auditing, control, or security and must complete another entry-level exam through the ISACA certification scheme. The certification covers high-level topics such as the information systems auditing process, governance and management of IT, operations and business resilience, and IS acquisition, development, and implementation.

The average salary for IT professionals with a CISA certification is $109,713 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $575 for ISACA members; $760 for non-members

CompTIA A+

CompTIA offers a variety of certifications for IT pros at every stage of their IT careers, and the CompTIA A+ certification is its entry-level IT certification covering the foundations of hardware, technical support, and troubleshooting. The certification is designed for those interested in a career as a service desk analyst, help desk tech, technical support specialist, field service technician, help desk technician, associate network engineer, data support technician, desktop support administrator, or end user computing technician. To earn your CompTIA A+ certification you’ll have to pass two separate exams. The CompTIA A+ 220-1001 exam covers mobile devices, networking technology, hardware, virtualization and cloud computing, and network troubleshooting. The CompTIA A+ 220-1002 exam covers installing and configuring operating systems, expanded security, software troubleshooting, and operational procedures. While it is an entry-level certification, it’s recommended to have at least 9 to 12 months of hands-on experience in the field.

The average salary for entry-level IT professionals with a CompTIA A+ certification is $41,659 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $274 for exam voucher

CompTIA Cloud+

The CompTIA Cloud+ certification is designed to validate that cloud professionals have the skills necessary to maintain and optimize cloud infrastructure services. The exam is vendor-neutral and covers several relevant vendors so you can gain a larger picture of cloud infrastructure services. You’ll learn and be tested on configurations and deployment, management of cloud resources, maintenance of systems, security, and troubleshooting. It’s recommended to have at least two to three years of experience in system administration before taking the exam.

The average salary for IT professionals with a CompTIA Cloud+ certification is $128,365 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $399 for exam voucher

CompTIA Security+

The CompTIA Security+ certification is best suited for network, system, and security administrators; security specialists; junior IT auditors; security consultants; and security engineers. Security is a priority for nearly every business — as technology becomes a top driver of business success, companies are looking for qualified IT pros who can help ensure that they are protected from potential threats and risks. The certification exam covers topics such as threats, attacks, vulnerabilities, risk management, architecture and design, technology and tools, cryptography and PKI, and identity and access management.

The average salary for IT professionals with a CompTIA Security+ certification is $55,353 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $439 for exam voucher

IBM AI Engineering Professional Certificate

The IBM AI Engineering Professional Certificate is a free 13-course series aimed at mid-level employees who are interested in preparing for or advancing a career as a machine learning engineer. This intermediate-level certificate program covers everything you’ll need to know about machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, ML algorithms, and how to build deep learning modals and neural networks using tools such as Keras, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. IT professionals can gain the necessary hands-on, practical experience with in-demand AI tools that employers are hiring for through this certificate program. Participants in the program will get experience building deep learning models and neural networks, creating LLMs, developing transfer learning applications in NLP, and constructing a QA bot using LangChain and LLM — walking away with a resume-ready portfolio to show employers.

Exam fee: Free

The average salary for IT professionals with an IBM AI Engineering Professional certificate is $102,938 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Microsoft Certified Azure Solutions Architect

The Microsoft Azure Solutions Architect certification validates your subject matter expertise in designing cloud and hybrid solutions on Azure, including network, compute, monitoring, storage, and security. It’s offered at the associate level, which tests your skills with implementing, monitoring, and managing an organization’s Microsoft Azure environment. Once you earn the associate level designation, you can take the test to earn your expert level certification. At the expert level, you’ll need advanced experience and deep knowledge of IT operations comprising networking, governance, disaster recovery, data platforms, virtualization, business continuity, identity, and security to pass the exam.

The average salary for IT professionals with the Microsoft Certified Azure Solutions Architect expert level certification is $146,601 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $165

Project Management Professional (PMP)

The Project Management Professional certification offered by PMI validates your project leadership experience and expertise, and demonstrates your capabilities to help organizations work more efficiently. The exam covers topics such as managing conflict, building and leading effective teams, training and empowering team members and stakeholders, executing projects to deliver business value, assessing and managing risks, and planning and managing budgets and resources, among others. For more about the PMP, and tips on how to pass it, see PMP certification: How to ace the Project Management Professional exam.

The average salary for IT professionals with a PMP certification is $122,388 per year, according to data from ZipRecruiter.

Exam fee: $425 for members; $675 for non-members

More on IT certifications:

  • The 20 most valuable IT certifications today
  • 17 best entry-level IT certifications to launch your career
  • 10 most popular IT certifications
  • 10 IT certifications paying the highest premiums today
  • 10 hottest IT certifications today
  • ITIL certification guide: Costs, requirements, levels, and paths

item.title: Jev and the era of model Tetris
item.description:
This spring, in an interview after a keynote, I said we were all playing LLM Tetris now. The days of using the same LLM for every agent problem were over. Some decisions needed to come back in milliseconds, and some could take three minutes. Some needed generative output, and some needed logical decisions where an open-weight model might do. Fit the model to the use case.

I still believe that. But I was only half right, because I was still picturing every piece as an LLM. Bigger or smaller, pricier or cheaper, faster or slower, but all the same shape: text in, text out.

On September 15, a model shipped that doesn’t write anything. Within three weeks, more than a dozen others followed, from OpenAI, Cloudflare and Perplexity to open-source projects you can run on a laptop. Then on October 27, we got yet another class of model from Liquid AI, small enough to run on a phone.

The game I described in the spring is real. It just has more piece shapes than I expected, and it isn’t only an LLM game anymore. It’s model Tetris now.

What a System One model actually is

The model is called Jev, from a startup called TypeSafe AI. Its founder, Diogo Almeida, says he helped build the instruction-following research at OpenAI that became ChatGPT. He then spent two years in stealth on a different question: if models have been superhuman at chat for years, where is all the automation?

His answer borrows from Daniel Kahneman’s Thinking, Fast and Slow. System Two is slow and deliberate. System One is fast and intuitive. Today’s frontier LLMs, with their reasoning traces and multi-second responses, live in System Two. But a lot of the decisions software makes all day are System One decisions: route this ticket, score this risk, take this branch.

A System One model doesn’t generate text. You hand it a piece of state and a set of typed questions, and it returns structured answers with calibrated probabilities. There are three question types: a Choice among options you define, a Score on a rubric you write and a yes-or-no probability TypeSafe calls a Noul. TypeSafe calls it a frontier-intelligence function call. I think of it as a smart if-statement.

The launch numbers are aggressive: $0.042 per million input tokens, output free and responses in 70 to 500 milliseconds.

One claim needs precision. TypeSafe says Jev can’t hallucinate. What that means is it can’t return an answer outside your schema. It can still pick the wrong answer from inside it, and it will tell you how confident it was when it did.

Then there’s the detail I enjoyed most. TypeSafe named Jev after William Stanley Jevons, because it expects machine intelligence to follow coal’s path: every drop in the cost of intelligence unlocks more uses for it. Longtime readers know I’ve leaned on Jevons Paradox to explain why bank tellers multiplied after ATMs and why AI coding agents haven’t emptied out engineering teams. Now somebody has named a model after it.

Three weeks that made it a category

One model is a product. What happened next made it a category.

At its DevDay in late September, OpenAI previewed a Decisions API built on GPT-6 Luna. On October 6, it opened it to all developers in public beta at $0.10 per million input tokens, with output free, and says it decides roughly ten times faster than the same model through its regular API. On October 1, Cloudflare released Clef, open-weight decision models whose smaller version returns a median decision in under 40 milliseconds. Perplexity opened its own Decisions API the same day, also on open weights, and claimed a narrow win over Jev on its own benchmark panel. Amazon’s Strands Labs reportedly shipped an open-source decider that day too, and Liquid AI’s d1 and Upstage’s Solar Decide joined a growing list of open-source projects.

On October 2, llama.cpp, the engine behind a lot of local model serving, added an endpoint that speaks the same request format Jev introduced. Cloudflare’s Clef speaks it too.

Two things stand out for CIOs. First, the interface standardized before the market did. That’s how containers made runtimes interchangeable, how MCP made tools accessible for agents, and it matters for what I’ll argue below. Second, published prices range from $0.02 to $0.24 per million input tokens across vendors. When prices for the same kind of thing span an order of magnitude, nobody knows what it really costs yet. TypeSafe itself says it can’t prove its pricing isn’t subsidized and the pricing tier here will be something to keep an eye on.

Why I taught three agents to play Pac-Man

I don’t know of any customers running System One models in production yet. The category is barely two months old. So, I did what I’d tell any CIO to do with a new piece: I tried it. And I tried it with a use case that seems like a toy until you think about it a little bit.

I’m building agents to play Pac-Man. Why? That’s a use case that requires good decisions made quickly, where broader context and planning matter and everybody understands success metrics. You clear the board or you don’t. You score points or you get eaten by a ghost.

What I wanted to learn wasn’t only which model knew the most, which is a knowledge question. What I wanted to test was: is a quick decision that might not be optimal worth more than a better one that takes longer? You can’t answer that on paper, because it depends on how fast the world changes underneath the decision. I had to try it to find out. So do you.

First I built the harness. Using Claude Code, I wired up MAME, the arcade emulator, so a program could play, and started with an agent that picked a random direction at every intersection. That agent was useless at Pac-Man and invaluable for everything else. It let me get observability right and settle on an ASCII version of the board as the agent’s input before any model was involved. Build the harness first, and trying three models becomes cheap. It’s the lesson I took from software engineering in July: the scaffolding is what makes testing possible.

The game sends a new board state roughly every 17 milliseconds. Even a local open-weight model on my M4 Mac couldn’t weigh tactics and strategy in one shot at that pace. So, I split the work into two loops, last month’s micro-agent pattern in miniature. A tactical loop decides which way to turn, given the current goal. A planning loop picks the goal from 11 options: clear a quadrant, go for one of the energizers, hunt, escape or finish the level.

Then I built three planners on the same tactical loop. code-planner picks a goal with a proximity analysis of the board, in plain code. jev-planner sends the board to Jev. haiku-planner sends it to Claude Haiku through Anthropic’s API. Both hosted models answered faster than the local open-weight options I tried.

I ran each one 100 times:

A decision has a shelf life

Look at the last column. The outcomes rank exactly with latency. Code-planner missed no frames, jev-planner missed about a third of a second’s worth, and haiku-planner missed close to a full second. Scores fell in the same order.

I don’t think Jev beat Haiku because it was smarter. I think it beat Haiku because it answered sooner. Watching the runs side by side, the losses look alike: a planner sticks with a quadrant too long, or switches to escape a beat too late. In one run, both model-driven planners got within a handful of dots of clearing the board and died chasing the last stranded pockets, while code-planner was already on level two.

A correct answer delivered after the window closes is a wrong answer. Pac-Man makes the window visible because it’s measured in frames and the penalty is a life. Enterprises have the same windows; they’re just harder to see. A card authorization has to clear in a fraction of a second. An ad bid expires. A guardrail sits in front of every request. A tool dispatch inside an agent loop gets paid for at every hop, which is the compounding I described in June.

The latency budget belongs on the list of criteria for choosing a model, right next to accuracy and cost. Most teams leave it off.

How to play model Tetris

The ordering that falls out of this is simple. If the rules are known and stable, write code. If the answer is one of a known set of options but the rules are too fuzzy to write by hand, use a System One model. If the answer has to be written, or the reasoning has to be explained, use an LLM and accept the wait. It’s too early to provide guidance on the new Liquid AI models, but this emerging class of smaller compute footprint cousins to the GPU-hungry LLMs may earn a place in a decision matrix as well.

One size does not fit all. Adapt to what best fits your use case, which is almost certainly different from my toy Pac-Man experiment.

To sort any given decision, ask four questions:

  1. Output shape. Does the answer have to be written, or can it be chosen from options you define in advance?
  2. Latency budget. Does it need to come back in milliseconds, or is three minutes fine?
  3. Explainability. Does someone downstream need to know why? A System One model returns a probability, not a rationale.
  4. Stakes. Is a calibrated threshold, with a human catching the uncertain cases, safer than one confident guess?

Run last month’s five-agent software delivery chain through those questions and the board fills in. Turning a business request into a technical issue needs an LLM. Point poker estimation is a Score. A merge gate is a yes-or-no probability. Test failure triage is a Choice. And some of it, honestly, is an if-statement.

Now the part that matters most: don’t limit your options. As an industry, we’ve been building databases for about 60 years. We’ve been building agents for about 18 months. System One models didn’t exist two months ago. Nobody should be confident that today’s model usage pattern will still be the right one 18 months from now.

Tetris makes the point better than I can. You only get a short preview of the next piece. A board built so it only works if the long straight piece shows up is a board that loses.

In practice, that means keeping the model choice behind an interface you control. My Pac-Man harness does this by design: three planners plug into the same tactical loop, and swapping one touches nothing else. The market is helping, too, since a dozen vendors converged on one decision API in three weeks. This is the deployment flexibility gap I described in May and the portability question from June. Lock-in used to be denominated in egress fees. Now it’s denominated in model usage patterns.

The piece every model still needs

Whatever pieces you play, one thing doesn’t change: every model is only as good as the state you hand it.

A System One model given the wrong context returns a calibrated, confident, wrong answer. Because it’s cheap, it can do that at enormous volume. Cloudflare’s hosted Clef currently reads only about the first 2,000 tokens of text state. In September I argued that the real question is which 200K tokens of a possible million earn their place. At 2K, that question gets much sharper.

The relationship runs both ways. Decision models are good at retrieval’s own hardest jobs: reranking candidates, filtering passages and checking whether a source actually supports a claim. Two of the retrieval practices from that September piece, reranking and knowing when to stop, are a Choice and a yes-or-no question. The new piece can help you play the rest of the board.

Here’s where Jevons comes back. When a decision costs a fraction of a cent and returns in milliseconds, enterprises won’t make the same decisions more cheaply. They’ll make far more of them. Every ticket, every retrieved chunk, every agent step gets scored, because now it can. More decisions mean more state to assemble, and retrieval quality at low operational and developer cost becomes the bottleneck.

That’s the next test for my Pac-Man agents. I’m adding memory, including retrieving board states from past deaths when the current board looks similar. If the right memories make a fast planner smarter without making it slower, that’s the retrieval argument with a score attached.

Objections

“Isn’t keeping every option open just model sprawl with a better name?” Not if the flexibility lives in the interface. Running every model at once is sprawl. Being able to swap one in an afternoon is flexibility.

“Isn’t this just a zero-shot classifier?” Partly. What’s new is calibrated confidence at near-frontier accuracy, behind a standard API, at a price low enough to run on every row of a table.

“A video game isn’t an enterprise workload.” Agreed. It’s a workload with a visible deadline. Plenty of enterprise workloads have deadlines too; they just don’t flash GAME OVER when they miss one.

The honest caveat

Nearly every benchmark in this category so far is vendor-reported, and TypeSafe’s own launch post notes its workflow evaluations were written by its own team. The pricing may be subsidized. A probability with no rationale is a real audit problem in regulated work, so expect System One models to route and screen rather than decide alone wherever someone has to explain why. And where a decision has no deadline, like a contract review or a quarterly forecast, three minutes is fine and the better answer should win. Fast doesn’t beat smart. Fast beats late.

The board

In the spring I said we were all playing LLM Tetris. The game turned out to be bigger than that. There are more piece shapes, they’re arriving faster and the board speeds up the longer you play. It’s broader, model Tetris now.

The teams that win won’t be the ones who found the perfect piece. They’ll be the ones who know the shape of each decision, put a latency budget next to accuracy and cost, feed every piece the right state, and keep the board flexible enough for whatever comes next.

And sometimes, as my code-planner keeps reminding me, the best piece on the board is an if-statement.

item.title: OffSec Celebrates 20 Years of Practitioner-Built Training From the Creators of Kali Linux and OSCP
item.description:
Meet the rest of OffSec as the company brings its hands-on approach to entire cyber teams.

Kali Linux. OSCP. Try Harder. For 20 years, OffSec has set the standard for the tools security practitioners use, the skills they prove, and the mindset they bring to the work. This month OffSec is marking its 20th anniversary as a global leader in hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications for individuals and enterprise security teams. 

“Our founders built an incredible brand and an incredible product,” said OffSec CEO Ning Wang. “Our mission has stayed the same. We develop critical thinkers, cyber warriors, and problem solvers who are ready to excel in their jobs under stress. Hands-on is the only way we believe you can effectively train someone.”

Built by the People Who Do the Work

OffSec began in 2006 when cybercrime was becoming big business. OffSec grew out of the security community, founded by practitioners who believed the best way to teach cybersecurity was to share what they’d learned through hands-on experience. That origin story still shapes how OffSec develops cybersecurity practitioners and teams. Through hands-on training with real systems, learners build practical skills, strengthen their problem-solving abilities, and gain the confidence to tackle challenges when the obvious approach fails.

The Tools Practitioners Use

BackTrack Linux brought penetration testing tools together in one open-source platform. In 2013, OffSec rebuilt it as Kali Linux, a free environment for penetration testing, research, forensics, and reverse engineering. In 2023, Kali Purple extended it to defenders.

The Standard Practitioners Prove Themselves Against

OSCP earned its reputation as the gold standard in penetration testing certifications because candidates must work through live systems, adapt their approach, and document what they accomplish. Employers trust it as evidence of real capability. For many practitioners, it is a career-defining milestone. OSCP+ added a renewable credential in 2024. Now, for a limited time, individual practitioners can save 20% off of Learn One annual subscription.

The Research and Practice They Learn From

In 2009, OffSec launched the Exploit Database, a non-profit, public-service archive of public exploits, proof-of-concept (PoC) code, shellcode, and security papers, which it still maintains as a free resource. It also acquired the open-source training project VulnHub, offers free labs in Proving Grounds Play, and recently added HackTrack. HackTrack offers live weekly training over a 10-week stretch. The first round of HackTrack focused on OSCP and was offered free to those with a Learn One or Course and Certification Bundle. A new HackTrack focused on OSAI is set to launch soon. 

Along the way, Try Harder became the security community’s shorthand for the persistence and dedication that a career in cybersecurity demands. In October 2026 at Singapore International Cyber Week, CEO Wang urged her Women in Cyber keynote audience to do hard things early that build confidence and resilience, noting, “If you don’t struggle through something, you will never become really great at it,” she said. 

The Technology Looks Different. The Challenge Feels Familiar

Attackers now use AI to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at speeds unimaginable 20 years ago. The time between a vendor patch and a working exploit continues to shrink. Cybersecurity skills gaps remain a growing challenge. According to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 95% of organizations report at least one skills gap, with 59% describing those gaps as critical or significant, up from 44% in 2024. These findings reinforce the need to move beyond once-a-year training toward continuous, hands-on skill development, an approach rooted in OffSec’s philosophy since day one.

“Frontier AI models are evolving at unbelievable speed. If you don’t keep up, you won’t be able to do the job,” said CEO Wang. “Certification still assesses capability. But you need to constantly upskill your teams so they are ready to defend your organization. It is simply no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Meet the Rest of Offsec: Training for the Whole Security Team

OffSec has grown from a specialist offensive security provider into a full cybersecurity learning and workforce development portfolio. Every course teaches the why, the what, and the how so practitioners learn to think through problems they have never seen. Through Learn Enterprise, OffSec’s hands-on training platform for enterprise security teams, organizations bring that approach to every member of their security team. The platform includes:

  • 14 certifications from foundational to expert level
  • 125+ customizable learning paths
  • 750+ labs
  • 8,000+ hours of content
  • Framework mapping to NICE, DCWF, SCyWF, ECSF, and more
  • Flexible licenses
  • Workforce leadership reporting

In 2026, OffSec added Live Training, which brings its instructors on site to work with security teams in realistic scenarios. OffSec has provided this training to more than two dozen organizations and hundreds of learners. 

OffSec’s AI Training Priorities

CEO Wang calls AI-era learning OffSec’s top priority. “To fight AI you have to use AI,” said CEO Wang. “Your red team and your blue team both need to be AI literate. Next year, we will release new and updated courses that modernize our training for the AI age.”

Preview OffSec’s Learn Enterprise platform, then request a personalized demo to explore how it can support your team’s training goals at: https://www.offsec.com/business/enterprise-solutions/. 

About OffSec

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.
